entry.title: Fine-Tuning Four Small Local Models Against a Swift Validator Loop
entry.summary: How we fine-tuned Qwen3.5 4B, Gemma 4 E2B, and Qwen3-ASR 1.7B/0.6B on open datasets against LokalBot's Swift validator, plus what did not work.
entry.content:
Why fine-tune four small models

Stock small models are trained to be decent at everything, which makes them shaky on narrow app contracts. Inside LokalBot, four models carry the whole local workflow on a laptop: Qwen3.5 4B writes source-linked meeting notes, decisions, actions, and Personal Context memories; Qwen3-ASR 1.7B and 0.6B handle meeting transcription and push-to-talk dictation; and Gemma 4 E2B drives inline autocomplete.

In version 0.14.0, all four defaults moved to Apache-2.0 fine-tunes published on Hugging Face. Every row in the training data comes from open-license sources (Apache-2.0, ODC-By-1.0, CC-BY-4.0, MIT, and CC0) plus open-weight teacher outputs. Zero private user meetings or recordings were used in training, and every previous stock model stays selectable in Settings > Models if you want to switch back.

1. Qwen3.5 4B (LokalBot v4): training inside the Swift validator loop

LokalBot's meeting pipeline already has a strict Swift evidence and ownership validator in MeetingNotesReplayTests. Every extracted action or decision must cite real transcript segments and assign an owner supported by the text. Early synthetic datasets looked fine to a generic judge and then failed inside the Swift app.

For v4, we ran every synthetic training meeting through the exact compiled Swift validator until all 4,117 rows passed with zero Swift rejections: 2,005 meetings (9,192 actions, 1.4% zero-action rate), 240 on-policy repair examples, 964 Personal Context memory cases (67.8% negative/empty traps), 338 Ask tool-calling trajectories, 170 Day Digest rows, and 400 general replay rows from allenai/tulu-3-sft-mixture.

That loop also exposed a real failure in v3: our synthetic meetings always had named speakers and a confirmed Me track, while real calls often arrive with unnamed diarized rosters (them 1..8, local 1..3, them unclear). That mismatch caused six zero-action collapses on our 28-meeting dev replay. Adding 487 unnamed diarized meetings in v4 brought those collapses to zero.

We trained a rank-32 bf16 LoRA across all 248 language-model linear projections, merged at scale=1.0 in fp32, and quantized to Q4_K_M (2.741 GB, matching stock byte range) with a 64-chunk bilingual English/Serbian/JSON imatrix. Same-GPU replay against stock Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M on pinned llama.cpp v1.0.0 with enable_thinking=false:

Qwen3.5-4B stock vs LokalBot v4 benchmark results
Suite & metricStock Qwen3.5 4BQwen3.5-4B-LokalBot-v4
Memory120 (Personal Context, 120 cases)81/120 (67.5%, 12 unwanted)118/120 (98.3%, 1 unwanted)
Memory120 Serbian recall (13 gold)0/13 (9 unwanted)13/13 (0 unwanted)
Blind21 completed jobs (21 untouched EN calls)20/2121/21
Blind21 validator rejections175 (56 repair passes)69 (-60.6%, 28 repair passes)
Blind21 median latency (G4 GPU)24.24 s13.64 s (1.78x faster)
Blind21 decision overlap (40 ref)3/40 (7.5%)18/40 (45.0%)
Blind21 raw action recall (85 ref)47/85 (55.3%)40/85 (47.1%, McNemar p=0.2478)
Private28 dev action recall / rejections73/147 (49.7%) / 160 rej76/147 (51.7%) / 67 rej (-58.1%)
Golden6 Russian drift on Serbian21 drift hits0 drift hits

What did not work: honest negative results

Publishing only the green rows makes local model numbers useless, so here are the two clearest misses from this cycle:

  • Blind21 raw action recall dropped versus stock. On the 21 untouched English holdout meetings, stock Qwen3.5-4B still recalled 47/85 (55.3%) reference actions compared to 40/85 (47.1%) for v4 (exact two-sided McNemar p = 0.2478), and stock produced fewer false-positive decisions on the 9 zero-decision meetings (6 vs 25). Also, when forced into enable_thinking=true on ThinkOnSmoke6, v4 passed 4/6 with one </think> tag leak, which is why LokalBot defaults v4 to thinking off under Automatic. We shipped v4 because 118/120 memory restraint, zero Serbian/Russian drift, 60.6% fewer validator rejections, and 1.78x faster extraction beat stock in day-to-day use, while keeping stock one click away.
  • The Astra weight-space pilot moved 5,120 weights and zero outputs. Before spending GPU hours on LoRA, I ran a bounded weight-editing pilot on Qwen3.5-4B using a rented RTX 3090 (~$0.14 GPU/disk cost). Guided by four dev traces, we halved two MLP output columns (2416 and 8819) in layers.23.mlp.down_proj.weight, editing 5,120 BF16 weights (27,741 packed bytes in blk.23.ffn_down.weight after Q4_K_M quantization). The tensor change survived quantization intact, and all 40 paired outputs (10 dev plus 30 held-out synthetic memory cases) came back byte-identical: 22/30 held-out on both arms, zero delta. Two edited columns could not shift behavior on this task; a full rank-32 LoRA across all 248 projections did.

2. Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (v3) and 0.6B (v1): killing silence ghosts and code-switching errors

Stock Qwen3-ASR 1.7B had two bugs that showed up immediately in daily use. First, holding the dictation shortcut in a quiet room with a custom vocabulary prompt caused it to echo the prompt or hallucinate speech (only 8.3% clean silence on our holdout, with 16 prompt echoes and 123 hallucinated words). Second, mid-sentence bilingual code-switching (sr+en and en+de) hit 37.12% WER.

A decoder-only LoRA (v2) fixed dictation silence, but far-field meeting audio barely budged. For Qwen3-ASR-1.7B-LokalBot-v3, we unlocked the top 4 audio_tower transformer layers (layers.20..23) plus audio_tower.proj1 and proj2 with a rank-16 LoRA at a 0.4x differential learning rate alongside the rank-32 decoder LoRA (scale=1.15), anchored with Forward KL on guard languages so English, German, French, Spanish, and Russian would not drift.

  • Code-switching holdout WER (sr+en, en+de): cut from 37.12% to 12.81% (-24.31 pp).
  • Dictation silence & ambient noise: 100.0% clean abstention (0 prompt echoes, 0 hallucinated words, up from 8.3% / 123 words on stock). Custom vocabulary recall rose from 86.7% to 100.0% (4.00% WER vs 9.00%) with zero distractor injections.
  • South Slavic (sr/hr/bs) auto WER: dropped from 24.64% to 17.79% (-6.85 pp); out-of-domain Croatian (VoxPopuli hr) fell from 24.95% to 19.06%.
  • Expanded AMI-400 meetings (200 ihm + 200 sdm): close-mic 9.79% vs 10.24% stock; far-field 24.41% vs 26.08% (-1.67 pp), at 31.24x real-time on Apple M4 Max Metal (2.52 GB combined Q8_0 decoder and mmproj). Tradeoff: 2/200 low-SNR far-field clips abstain vs 0/200 stock, and guard languages shifted +0.18 pp (4.35% to 4.53%).

For smaller machines, Qwen3-ASR-0.6B-LokalBot-v1 (1.02 GB combined, 52.7x real-time on M4 Max Metal) keeps the audio_tower frozen so the stock mmproj stays bit-identical. On the same 466-clip blind holdout, it cut South Slavic auto WER from 52.26% to 30.57% (-21.69 pp), code-switching WER from 49.21% to 20.72% (-28.49 pp), raised custom vocabulary recall from 80.0% to 100.0% with 100% clean silence, and beat stock on AMI-400 (10.72% ihm, 26.23% sdm) while holding 7 guard languages within +0.13 pp.

3. Gemma 4 E2B (LokalBot v4): 56/56 context grounding at 20.2 ms

Inline autocomplete has the opposite problem from chat models: raising recall slightly too aggressively makes the ghost text annoying. Our earlier high-coverage checkpoint (v3) boosted word-boundary recall to 30.71%, but added +39 wrong-shown suggestions and missed 2 of 26 memory recall checks.

For Gemma-4-E2B-LokalBot-v4 (3.845 GB i1-Q6_K), we trained a rank-32 LoRA across 275 matrices in all 35 layers (including 70 Per-Layer Embedding projections) on 45,876 open-license rows using a three-regime Forward KL objective: soft-logit distillation from google/gemma-4-26B-A4B on ungrounded text, grounded window/memory rows, plus 13,400 KL-only calibration anchor rows against stock E2B starting at body token 0.

  • Context and memory grounding: 56/56 (100%) across all 7 saved-memory and visible-window suites (8/8 visible dev, 18/18 visible held-out, 4/4 link, 6/6 memory dev, 22/22 memory held-out, 12/12 relevance held-out), with zero stale facts and zero unsafe outputs across 28 safety checks.
  • Precision without chatter: 199 right / 182 wrong shown vs 182 / 181 on stock (+17 right completions for +1 wrong), raising email precision from 74.3% to 80.0%.
  • Latency: 20.2 ms median boundary latency and 80.0 ms typing p95 on M4 Max Metal (faster than stock 21.2 ms / 103.5 ms). Tradeoff: v4 still has 2 forbidden hits on fresh_holdout_v1 and 1 on fresh_holdout_v2; v3 stays in the repo for users who want maximum coverage.

Download the Apache-2.0 GGUFs

All four checkpoints are Apache-2.0 and work directly with llama-server, Ollama, or LokalBot 0.14.0:

  • Think (notes, actions, memory, Ask): stevyhacker/Qwen3.5-4B-LokalBot-GGUF (Qwen3.5-4B-LokalBot-v4-Q4_K_M.gguf, 2.74 GB)
  • Transcription (accuracy): stevyhacker/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B-LokalBot-GGUF (v3 Q8_0 + paired mmproj, 2.52 GB)
  • Transcription (compact): stevyhacker/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B-LokalBot-GGUF (v1 Q8_0 + stock mmproj, 1.02 GB)
  • Autocomplete (Cotyping): stevyhacker/Gemma-4-E2B-LokalBot-GGUF (Gemma-4-E2B-LokalBot-v4-i1-Q6_K.gguf, 3.85 GB)

Fresh installs of LokalBot 0.14.0 pick these defaults automatically. Existing installs keep their current models until you click Upgrade on Today or in Settings > Models. See the full reproducible numbers across every local role on our Local Desktop AI Leaderboard.

entry.title: 39 ms and 50 MB vs. 255 ms and 1 GB: benchmarking local meeting retrieval on QMSum
entry.summary: Comparing LokalBot's SQLite FTS5 + EmbeddingGemma 2 retrieval against GBrain on 232 QMSum meetings and 1,576 questions: recall, latency, and RAM.
entry.content:
Why we ran this

Every few weeks a new local memory layer promises better recall for coding agents and personal assistants. LokalBot's own retrieval is intentionally plain: SQLite FTS5 BM25 plus EmbeddingGemma 2 (310 MB, 768 dimensions) joined with reciprocal rank fusion. We tested whether replacing it with GBrain (v0.60.734.0 on PGLite over stdio MCP) improved meeting recall enough to justify the extra runtime.

The setup

We used the public QMSum corpus (232 meetings, 129,177 turns, 2.1 million words across AMI product design, ICSI research, and parliamentary committees) and all 1,576 specific questions with human-marked answer spans. No personal data was used. Both systems ingested the exact same meetings and shared one local llama-server:embeddinggemma-2 instance on an Apple M4 Max (48 GB). Confidence intervals come from 2,000 paired bootstrap resamples over questions.

Results

Retrieval comparison on 1,576 QMSum questions (Apple M4 Max)
MetricLokalBot keywordGBrain keywordLokalBot hybridGBrain hybrid
Meeting R@10.1930.2530.2800.239
Meeting R@40.3350.4120.4750.367
Meeting R@100.4560.4680.5950.370
MRR0.2740.3250.3790.295
Gold turn in evidence0.2600.4020.3670.340
Median evidence handed to LLM718 chars97,444 chars1,248 chars96,761 chars
Query latency (p50 / p95)3 / 8 ms159 / 212 ms39 / 52 ms255 / 342 ms

What stood out

  • Hybrid retrieval favored LokalBot cleanly. With the same embedder, LokalBot led GBrain by +4.1 points on R@1 (95% CI +1.9 to +6.2) and +10.9 points on R@4 (+8.2 to +13.3), at 6.5× lower median latency (39 ms vs. 255 ms) and roughly 50 MB vs. 1 GB resident memory (excluding the shared 0.5 GB embedding server).
  • Context budget matters on local models. GBrain's default query hands back a median ~97,000 characters (full transcripts) per question. LokalBot hands back 1,248 characters (top 4 meetings, up to 6 moments of 400 characters each), which fits comfortably inside a local 4B model or a coding agent's MCP tool budget.
  • GBrain's keyword-only search beat LokalBot's keyword-only search. On lexical queries alone, GBrain hit R@1 0.253 vs. 0.193 and got the gold turn into evidence on 40.2% vs. 26.0% of questions. That points directly at an improvement we can take into LokalBot's FTS5 query formulation without adopting a heavier database.
  • Restated contradictions are still unsolved in both. Explicit edits and deletions worked cleanly in both systems (40/40 and 39/40), but when a later meeting silently reversed an earlier decision, neither ranked the newer meeting above the older one reliably (7/20 in LokalBot, 8/20 in GBrain).

Data and reproduction

The corpus builder, harness, scorer, and full report are in Benchmarks/memory/GBrain/2026-11-17/REPORT.md. A keyword-only repeat on a 4-core Intel Xeon produced identical accuracy numbers. See the benchmarks page for the rest of LokalBot's local stack.

entry.title: Local speech-to-text vs. cloud APIs on real meetings
entry.summary: Benchmarking local Qwen3-ASR 1.7B and Parakeet against Gemini, GPT-4o Transcribe, and Qwen-Audio cloud APIs on AMI meetings and two-track calls.
entry.content:
Why test against cloud APIs

People often assume running transcription on a laptop means trading away accuracy for privacy. We tested LokalBot's default local models—Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (8-bit) and Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 on an Apple M4 Max—head-to-head against direct API calls to OpenAI (gpt-transcribe, gpt-4o-transcribe, gpt-4o-mini-transcribe), Google (gemini-3.5-transcribe, gemini-3.8-flash), and Alibaba Model Studio (qwen-audio-3.1-asr-flash, qwen3-asr-flash).

Public AMI meetings (human reference)

Sixteen 90–120 second windows from four AMI Mix-Headset test meetings (27.4 minutes, 4,160 reference words), containing heavy overlapped speech on a single mixed channel:

AMI Mix-Headset WER comparison across cloud APIs and local models
SystemWER95% CILow-overlap WERList price / hrSpeed
Gemini 3.8 Flash (prompted)16.7%14.0–19.0%6.2%$0.2118×
Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (local)17.6%14.6–20.5%7.1%$044×
Qwen3-ASR Flash (API)18.1%14.6–20.8%6.3%$0.1325×
Qwen-Audio 3.1 ASR Flash18.5%14.6–21.8%5.6%$0.0210×
Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (local)19.2%15.8–22.3%8.1%$0129×
GPT-4o mini Transcribe21.8%17.5–25.7%7.8%$0.1834×
GPT Transcribe22.2%17.6–27.5%6.9%$0.2730×
GPT-4o Transcribe23.0%18.4–27.0%6.2%$0.3625×

Two-track real meetings: where cloud APIs broke

On 99 two-track chunks (69.9 minutes) from real meetings scored by cross-family ROVER consensus disagreement (measuring agreement, not human ground truth), local Qwen3-ASR 1.7B placed first at 4.2% disagreement (0.4 s median latency, 0 dropped spans), tied within confidence intervals with Gemini 3.5 Transcribe (4.5%, 6.3 s latency) and Qwen-Audio 3.1 ASR Flash (4.6%, 2.9 s latency).

Two failure modes jumped out immediately:

  • Gemini 3.8 Flash invented speech on quiet clips. Despite leading AMI WER by 0.9 points, on real meeting chunks it hallucinated 115 words across 15 spans—including turning a 1.2-second clip that every other system heard as one word or silence into a fluent 30-word sentence.
  • GPT-4o Transcribe silently dropped microphone speech. It logged 278 dropped words in runs of four or more and 42% disagreement on one meeting's microphone track (vs. 7–14% for the other systems). Only ~20% of those dropped words appeared on the system track, ruling out echo suppression.
  • Span length matters inside our own app. The test also caught a bug in LokalBot's older production path: cutting audio at speaker turns before transcription hurt AMI WER (26.5% vs. 17.7%). Assigning speakers after transcribing longer spans closed that gap.

Data and reproduction

Full tables, ROVER methodology, and caveats are in Benchmarks/transcribe/CloudSTT/results/2026-09-30/REPORT.md and the follow-up span-length report. Try the same local models offline in LokalBot.

entry.title: 56 ms local system-wide autocomplete: Gemma 4 E2B vs. LFM2.5 1.2B
entry.summary: Headless keystroke benchmark of local autocomplete: 56 ms median with Gemma 4 E2B vs 26 ms with LFM2.5 1.2B across 788 word positions.
entry.content:
Measuring autocomplete without fooling ourselves

Our original 28-scenario autocomplete check had five flaws: it treated an intentional confidence-gate silence as a safety failure, accepted only one exact word tail for partial-word completions, mixed 10–40 s cold startup into steady-state latency, stole keyboard focus by launching the full app, and never measured next-word accuracy.

We replaced it with a headless engine runner (--cotyping-bench) that exercises the exact production LlamaCotypingRuntime with hybrid decoding, certified prefix search, and prefix healing across 28 safety/behaviour checks (5 deterministic passes) plus 96 phrases replayed at all 788 word boundaries and 8 phrases typed one character at a time.

Gemma 4 E2B Base vs. LFM2.5 1.2B Instruct (Apple M4 Max)

Autocomplete engine benchmark comparing Gemma 4 E2B Base Q6_K and LFM2.5 1.2B Instruct Q4_K_M
MetricGemma 4 E2B Base (Balanced)LFM2.5 1.2B Instruct (Lightweight)
Unsafe results (28 checks × 5 passes)00
Word completions12 / 1312 / 13
Next-word accuracy (788 positions)23.1%20.7%
English accuracy (624 positions)25.3%24.2%
Non-English accuracy (164 positions)14.6%7.3%
Right when shown (precision)50.1%43.0%
Per keystroke while typing (median / p95)56 / 102 ms26 / 76 ms
Model load time0.65 s0.16 s

What the numbers actually say

  • In English, the two models are effectively tied (+1.1 points, 95% bootstrap interval −1.4 to +3.5), while LFM2.5 is 2–3× faster per keystroke (26 ms median) and weighs only 0.73 GB.
  • Gemma 4 E2B earns the Balanced default on precision and non-English text. When it chooses to show a suggestion, it is right 50.1% of the time vs. 43.0% for LFM2.5, and its non-English lead (+7.3 points) comes largely from languages like Serbian where LFM2.5 stayed silent.
  • Silence is a feature. Both models withheld suggestions on the exact same 3 open-ended prompts (notes-list, comma-clause, sentence-start) and stayed quiet mid-word (rec|eive), producing zero unsafe suggestions across all 140 passes.

First suggestion after a pause (November 18, 2026)

Steady-state speed only tells half the story: after three minutes without a decode, llama.cpp releases Metal weight residency (180 s default keep-alive), and the GPU clocks down within seconds. On an M4 Max (Gemma 4 E2B Q6_K), warming the runtime with a single throwaway token on wake, unlock, click, or the first keystroke (then removing that token so the cached prompt stays intact) brings the first suggestion back to steady-state latency:

First suggestion latency after idle pauses on Apple M4 Max (Gemma 4 E2B Q6_K)
Idle pauseBeforeWarm-up at keyWarm-up just beforeWarm reference
20 s61 ms51 ms47 ms46–50 ms
60 s59 ms48 ms50 ms48–50 ms
300 s (5 min)95–130 ms50–53 ms49 ms47–49 ms

Four warm-up touches over a five-minute pause added 18 mJ of CPU energy (468 vs. 450 mJ) and never reload a model freed under memory pressure. A 30-minute pause under memory pressure—where OS file paging dominates—has not been re-measured yet. Full methodology and raw logs live in Benchmarks/autocomplete/Cotyping/results/2026-11-18-first-after-pause/REPORT.md.

Choosing between them in LokalBot

Both presets ship built into LokalBot: Balanced local uses Gemma 4 E2B Base, and Lightweight local switches to LFM2.5 1.2B Instruct for faster typing and a smaller disk footprint. For a feature-by-feature comparison with Cotypist and Cotabby, see Autocomplete that knows your meetings. Full category breakdowns and commands to rerun the engine harness are in Benchmarks/autocomplete/Cotyping/results/2026-10-15-engine-benchmark/REPORT.md.

entry.title: Recall vs. restraint: which local models know when not to save a memory
entry.summary: 120-case benchmark of local models saving personal memories and abstaining on traps: Qwen3.5 4B/9B, Hy-Memory 30B, LFM2.5 24B, and MemT-1.0-Nano.
entry.content:
Why restraint matters

LokalBot's Personal Context learns facts, preferences, goals, and principles from what you type and say, so that agents you allow can tailor their work to you. A missed memory costs little: the next conversation usually brings it up again. A wrong one is worse. It quietly ends up in the context every agent reads, and nobody notices until an answer is off.

So the test asks for both recall and restraint. Three kinds of cases make the difference visible:

  • Who said it. “I live in Valencia” should be saved. “My colleague said, ‘I live in Valencia’” should not.
  • Already known. A new preference should be saved. One already in the known-memories list should be skipped.
  • Policy. A job title mentioned alongside a salary should be kept, and the salary left out.

The test

The benchmark has 120 synthetic cases arranged as 60 contrast pairs. The main comparison uses the 96 English cases: 52 contain one useful memory to extract, and in 44 the correct output is an empty list. A separate 24-case Serbian slice is reported on its own.

Every model received the same application prompt with its native chat template, an enforced JSON schema, temperature 0, seed 0, thinking disabled, and a single pass, with no model-specific prompt tuning. The GGUF models ran one after another through llama.cpp on the same Ryzen 7 9700X server. This measures accuracy, not speed. A recalled memory only counts when it also cites the right source line.

Results

Results on the 96 English cases
ModelUseful memories recalledUnwanted proposalsEmpty cases correct
Qwen3.5 4B, Q4_K_M30/52 (57.7%)342/44 (95.5%)
Qwen3.5 9B, Q4_K_M37/52 (71.2%)540/44 (90.9%)
Hy-Memory 30B-A3B, official Q4_K_M52/52 (100%)760/44 (0%)
LFM2.5 24B-A2B, QAD Q4_040/52 (76.9%)5310/44 (22.7%)
MemT-1.0-Nano, NF4 experts / BF16 dense51/52 (98.1%)639/44 (88.6%)

What stood out

  • Perfect recall can hide the real problem. Hy-Memory captured every eligible memory and failed all 44 cases where the right answer was nothing, with 76 unwanted proposals. Scored on recall alone, it would look like the best model here.
  • The Qwen models held back. Both missed more valid memories, but they handled over 90% of the empty cases and made only three and five unwanted proposals.
  • LFM2.5 copied from the instructions. In several cases it proposed “I live in Belgrade”, an example from the prompt with no support in the conversation. It also often returned the source sentence instead of the required source-line ID. Accepting exact quotations recovered 9 of its 18 invalid English citations, raising exact source selection from 51 to 56 of 96 cases, but that only repairs formatting. The table keeps the strict scoring.
  • MemT-1.0-Nano was the best balance. A reader on r/LocalLLaMA suggested it, and it was added on October 25: 51 of 52 useful memories, 6 unwanted proposals, and 39 of 44 empty cases. On the Serbian slice it recalled 13 of 13, made 3 unwanted proposals, and passed 8 of 11 empty cases, but three of its outputs switched language or script.

Caveats

  • MemT-1.0-Nano ran with experimental NF4 expert offload through Transformers on a Radeon RX 6600 XT; the other models ran as GGUF files in llama.cpp on a CPU. There is no matched run of its Qwen3.6-35B-A3B backbone, so the comparison isn't controlled for hardware or precision.
  • Each case starts from a fresh state, so MemT's persistent memory feature isn't exercised.
  • An AI assistant wrote the cases and graded the semantic decisions with the model names visible. There is no independent human validation and no claim of statistical significance.

What it means for LokalBot

These results don't change LokalBot's defaults. What they confirm is that a memory writer has to be judged on what it leaves out as much as on what it finds. The suggestions Personal Context learns appear under To review in Settings → Personal Context, where you keep or dismiss them.

Data

Everything needed to check or rerun the comparison is in the repository: the benchmark folder with the cases, prompts, and scorer, the MemT report with every failed case, and the raw responses. Other model results are on the benchmarks page.

entry.title: LokalBot is on Windows and Linux, in alpha
entry.summary: LokalBot adds a native Rust and GPUI app for Windows and Linux: local meeting notes, dictation, autocomplete, and search sharing the Mac library format.
entry.content:
What works

Updated November 3, 2026: most features that were Mac only when this post came out have since been ported, so these lists describe the app as it is now.

The Windows and Linux app is written in Rust with GPUI, the UI framework behind the Zed editor. Meetings, transcription, Ask, search, day memory, screen context, dictation, autocomplete, selection actions, spoken summaries, Files, overnight review, Personal Context, meeting note and daily exports, calendar, Agent Mode, and the CLI and MCP server for coding agents all work. Like the Mac app, it runs its models on your computer by default, and it has no account and no telemetry.

What's still missing

  • The Windows build isn't code-signed yet. SmartScreen asks before the first launch: choose More info → Run anyway.
  • Wayland support is partial. Autocomplete in other apps works as an input method on Sway, Hyprland, GNOME, where you also add LokalBot as an input source, and, since 0.12.3, KDE Plasma, where you choose it under Virtual Keyboard. It has only been tried on headless Sway, GNOME, and KWin with stand-in suggestions, and Hyprland itself hasn't been run (how it works). On other compositors it works in the practice editor in Settings. For dictation and selection actions on Wayland, bind lokalbot dictate and lokalbot selection-actions to shortcuts in your desktop's settings.
  • Meeting audio isn't always one app's. On Windows and Linux LokalBot records the meeting app alone where it can be separated, and otherwise everything the computer plays.
  • Remembered speakers only suggest. Later meetings offer a remembered name for you to apply, rather than naming the speaker automatically as on Mac.
  • No iPhone or iPad app yet. Android phones and tablets pair with Windows and Linux as they do with a Mac, through the app on Google Play, but the iPhone and iPad app isn't in the App Store yet.
  • A few features are Mac-only for now: Gmail in meeting briefs, Apple Intelligence, Granite Speech transcription, and Nemotron speaker separation.

The full list is in what works where, and the two-page overview shows what changed.

The models

  • Transcription: Qwen3-ASR 0.6B through sherpa-onnx, with Parakeet v3 and v2, SenseVoice, GigaAM for Russian, and Whisper turbo as options.
  • Speaker separation: pyannote segmentation and TitaNet.
  • Notes and Ask: Qwen3.5 4B, the same as on Mac.
  • Search: EmbeddingGemma 2, the same as on Mac.
  • Autocomplete: LFM2.5 1.2B.

The default download is about 4 GB. llama.cpp runs on a Vulkan GPU or the CPU, and since 0.11.3 you can choose CUDA (experimental) in Settings → Models → llama.cpp on a supported NVIDIA GPU. You can swap any model in Settings.

Install

  • Windows 10 or 11, x64: run LokalBot-<version>-windows-x86_64-setup.exe from the latest release. It installs for your user, without administrator rights. A portable zip is in the same release.
  • Linux x86_64: install the .deb (Debian, Ubuntu), the .rpm (Fedora, openSUSE), or the Arch package, or extract the .tar.gz and run ./install.sh. Since 0.11.2 the .deb, and the .rpm on Fedora, add the LokalBot repository, so sudo apt upgrade or sudo dnf upgrade brings later versions.

Linux needs glibc 2.39 or later (Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 13, Fedora 40, or newer), PulseAudio or PipeWire, and a Vulkan or OpenGL driver. See the system requirements.

On Omarchy and other Hyprland desktops

Omarchy already has everything LokalBot uses on Wayland: grim for screen context, wtype and wl-clipboard for dictation, PipeWire for meeting audio, and the Hyprland desktop portal. Install the Arch package with sudo pacman -U, then bind LokalBot's commands in ~/.config/hypr/bindings.lua. These keys are free in Omarchy's defaults:

o.bind("SUPER + ALT + D", "LokalBot dictation", "lokalbot dictate")
o.bind("SUPER + ALT + A", "Ask LokalBot", "lokalbot quick-recall")

The tray icon appears in Omarchy's bar, and the dictation pill and Quick Recall float instead of tiling.

Omarchy runs Fcitx 5 for typing other languages, and a desktop runs one input method at a time, so autocomplete in other apps stays out of its way and Settings says so. If you don't use Fcitx 5, systemctl --user disable --now omarchy-fcitx5.service lets autocomplete start. This comes from reading Omarchy's repository; it hasn't been tried on Omarchy.

Tell us what breaks

Most testing so far has been on a handful of personal and rented machines, so reports from real hardware help the most. Open an issue with your distribution, desktop, X11 or Wayland, CPU and GPU, and what you tried.

entry.title: How the Windows and Linux port was built
entry.summary: How coding agents ported 150,000 lines of Swift to Rust and GPUI in three days, how the result was verified, and a link to the full write-up.
entry.content:
A first attempt that only looked right

On October 2 a coding agent built a working Windows and Linux app with a native interface and CI on both platforms in one morning. It had its own data model and its own library on disk, so it couldn't open anything recorded on a Mac, and nothing would show when it drifted from how the Mac app behaves. That pull request was closed.

Specs before code

The second attempt spent its first hour on specs. Four agents read the Mac app's 150,000 lines of Swift without changing anything and wrote down the library format, the processing pipeline with every model prompt, every screen with its exact text, and the command-line tools and privacy rules. The core data types were written to match the Mac app's files, and every agent tested against a real library recorded by the Mac app. Six implementation agents then each took one part of the code.

How the work was checked

The port landed as one large pull request, so the checks mattered more than reading every line of the diff:

  • CI runs the app on a virtual display on Linux and on Windows and takes a screenshot of every page.
  • The live transcript is tested by playing a scripted conversation into virtual audio devices. That caught two bugs the unit tests had missed.
  • Autocomplete is tested by typing into Notepad and checking that the suggestion appears after the cursor.
  • End-to-end runs use the real models from an empty library: they download the models, process a short meeting, and ask a question about it.
  • Meetings recorded on a Mac are played on Linux, with their timestamps required to line up exactly.
  • Afterwards, the Mac and Windows/Linux apps were compared feature by feature, and the gaps were closed in five separate pull requests.

Read the full write-up

The full story, including the build machines, the rules for agents working side by side, and the decisions that were left to a person, is on Field Notes: Porting LokalBot to Linux and Windows with agents. The result is described in LokalBot is on Windows and Linux, in alpha.

entry.title: Autocomplete that knows your meetings
entry.summary: LokalBot's local autocomplete runs Gemma 4 E2B at ~56 ms median on an M4 Max and brings in recent meeting facts. Compared with Cotypist and Cotabby.
entry.content:
Fast enough to stay out of the way

Getting autocomplete to be useful without being intrusive or laggy took a lot of experiments with different models and quantizations. The best balance of suggestion quality and latency on a regular MacBook turned out to be the Gemma 4 E2B base model at 6-bit (Q6_K), running in-process through llama.cpp. On an M4 Max a suggestion takes a median of 56 ms while typing (see the full engine benchmark).

Update, November 19, 2026 — first suggestion after a pause: Cotypist highlights staying fast when you resume typing after a break. Previously, once llama.cpp's 180-second Metal residency keep-alive lapsed, LokalBot's first suggestion after a 5-minute pause took 95–130 ms. LokalBot now warms the loaded runtime with a single throwaway token on screen wake, unlock, click, or the first keystroke—removing that token afterward so the cached prompt stays intact—cutting a 5-minute pause down to 49–53 ms against a 47–49 ms warm reference (benchmark report; 30-minute pauses under heavy memory pressure remain unmeasured).

Context from your own work

  • The text above the field. On by default, read through macOS accessibility. Private browser windows are never read.
  • Your meetings, if you opt in. When your draft names something distinctive, LokalBot can add up to two facts from your own meeting notes to the model's context.

Autocomplete lives in the same app as meetings, dictation, and screen recall, which share one memory budget for their models.

How it compares

Cotypist and Cotabby are the closest local-first alternatives. As described on their sites (checked October 13, 2026; LokalBot column updated November 19, 2026):

Cotypist, Cotabby, and LokalBot autocomplete compared
FeatureCotypistCotabbyLokalBot
License and priceProprietary; free for 100 words a day, paid for unlimitedAGPL-3.0, free (beta)GPLv3, free, no limits
PlatformsmacOSmacOSmacOS (Swift), Windows & Linux (Rust + GPUI)
ModelLocal (Gemma 4 E4B recommended)Local GGUF through llama.cpp, or Apple IntelligenceGemma 4 E2B base Q6_K (Balanced) or LFM2.5 1.2B (Lightweight), in-process llama.cpp
First suggestion after a 5-min pauseAdvertised fast resumeNot published49–53 ms on M4 Max (warm-up on wake, click, or key)
Knows what was said in your meetingsNoNoYes, opt-in
Text above the fieldNot documented on its siteOCR of the windowAccessibility text, never from private windows
Also in the appAutocomplete onlyEmoji, macros, autocorrectMeetings, dictation, screen recall, read-only MCP

A head-to-head with Cotabby used identical inputs and the same Gemma 4 E2B weights over 782 next-word checkpoints. LokalBot predicted the exact next word 32.7% of the time (256 of 782) and Cotabby 30.7% (240 of 782), a difference of 2.0 points with a 95% interval of 0.0 to 4.0. In other words, the two are comparable on accuracy; the work now is on the experience around the suggestions.

Try it

Turn on Autocomplete in Settings → Writing. It needs the Accessibility and Input Monitoring permissions and a one-time model download. Tab accepts a word. Password fields and apps you exclude are never read.

entry.title: Search your meetings from Raycast
entry.summary: The LokalBot Raycast extension searches local meeting titles, summaries, and transcripts from Raycast without opening the app or using the network.
entry.content:
Two commands

  • Quick Recall. Type a word and see every meeting where it came up, from titles, summaries, or the transcript itself. Enter reveals the meeting's files in Finder and ⌘Enter copies the matching snippet.
  • Recent Meetings. Lists your last 20 meetings.

Local, like the app

The extension makes no network requests. It reads your local LokalBot library, and only after you allow external agents to read your meeting library in LokalBot's privacy settings.

It needs the LokalBot app installed, which on Mac means Apple Silicon and macOS 15 or later.

Install

Get LokalBot in the Raycast Store. It's the first LokalBot extension for Raycast, so tell us what's missing or annoying.

entry.title: Five local models, 6.8 GB of weights
entry.summary: Benchmarking every model in LokalBot shrank the 0.9.2 stack to 6.8 GB with faster notes, lower speaker error, and quicker local autocomplete.
entry.content:
Update, October 2026: two defaults have changed since this post. Search now uses EmbeddingGemma 2, and autocomplete uses Gemma 4 E2B; see Autocomplete that knows your meetings. Current numbers are on the benchmarks page.

The stack in 0.9.2

  • Transcription: Qwen3-ASR 1.7B, MLX 8-bit.
  • Who spoke when: Nemotron 3, Core ML.
  • Notes and action items: Qwen3.5 4B, Q4_K_M in llama.cpp.
  • Search embeddings: Harrier 0.6B, Q8_0.
  • Autocomplete in any app: LFM2.5 1.2B, Q4_K_M.
  • Screen text: Apple Vision OCR, opt-in.

What changed, in numbers

Measured on an M4 Max with 48 GB of memory:

  • A 26-minute meeting goes to finished notes in 33 seconds with the model already loaded, decoding at about 85 tokens a second.
  • Speaker error dropped from 43.4% to 14.6% diarization error rate on the AMI corpus. That's against the previous pyannote setup, so it says more about that configuration than about pyannote.
  • Autocomplete latency at the 95th percentile fell from 1.83 s with Gemma 4 E4B to 0.49 s.

A model that didn't make it

MiniCPM5 2B was tested for notes. It was smaller and faster, but it got stuck repeating itself on one summary and assigned action items to the wrong person. Qwen3.5 4B stayed the default: saving a few seconds isn't worth getting wrong who agreed to do what.

Also in the app

A read-only MCP server and CLI, off by default, let Claude Code or any other MCP client pull context from your meetings.

There are no numbers yet from 16 GB Macs or other M-series chips. If you run LokalBot on one, especially an M5 or M6, share what you get. The 0.9.2 release notes have the rest.

entry.title: A whole workday on local models
entry.summary: LokalBot 0.5 adds overnight Dreaming morning briefs, faster local autocomplete, and Quick Recall answers running locally on your Mac.
entry.content:
Update, October 2026: several default models have changed since this post; the current ones are on the benchmarks page.

What it does

  • Meetings. Detects Zoom, Teams, Meet, and other calls and records you and the other side on two synchronized tracks, with no bot joining the call. Transcription and the summary run on your Mac as soon as the meeting ends.
  • Dictation. Hold ⌥ Space, talk, and release. It's transcribed locally and pasted at the cursor, and the audio is deleted afterwards.
  • Autocomplete. Ghost-text suggestions in almost any Mac text field; Tab accepts. Opt-in.
  • Recall. Ask “what did we decide about this?” and get the answer from your own library, with the source meeting cited and the exact moment ready to replay. Full-text and semantic search cover everything.
  • Day timeline. An optional private timeline of where your time went, with a daily digest.

New in 0.5

  • Dreaming. LokalBot can compile a finished day overnight into a morning brief and structured work memory.
  • Faster autocomplete. New installs get the 0.73 GB LFM2.5 1.2B model, and accepting suggestions is more reliable across native apps, Chromium, and input methods.
  • Answers in Quick Recall. Quick Recall can answer right in its compact window instead of always opening the full Ask view.
  • Scheduled day digests, with a prompt you can customize.

The models in daily use

entry.title: Introducing LokalBot
entry.summary: LokalBot is a free, open-source app that records and summarizes meetings, autocompletes your typing, and tracks your day locally on your computer.
entry.content:
Update, October 2026: this is the original announcement. The default models have changed since (see Five local models, 6.8 GB of weights), the app now checks for updates (see the privacy policy for every network use), and LokalBot also runs on Windows and Linux.

One app instead of several

Recording meetings, autocompleting text, and keeping track of the day usually means several separate apps, each with its own subscription and its own cloud. LokalBot does all of it in one Mac app, with no third-party inference cost. It's free and open source under the GPLv3.

The model stack

  • Summaries, chat, and autocomplete run on a bundled llama.cpp: in-process for autocomplete's low latency, llama-server otherwise. Any of them can point at your own GGUF file, Ollama, an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or Apple Intelligence.
  • Transcription uses Granite Speech 4.1, Parakeet, Whisper, or Qwen3-ASR through Core ML and MLX on Apple Silicon. Parakeet runs at about 190 times real time.
  • Semantic search uses Qwen3-Embedding 0.6B on a second llama-server, with vectors in SQLite and brute-force cosine similarity. At personal scale, brute force is instant, and it adds no dependencies.
  • Speaker separation is optional: pyannote, through FluidAudio, splits the other side of a call into individual speakers.
  • An in-app Hugging Face browser searches and downloads GGUF models, with a note on whether each one fits your Mac.

Launch defaults

  • Transcription: IBM Granite Speech 4.1 2B, Q4.
  • Summaries: Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B, Q4_K_M.
  • Autocomplete: Gemma 4 E4B, Q5 XL.

These run well on an M4 Max with 48 GB of memory. With 16 to 24 GB, choose one of the lighter alternatives in the app's model settings.

Private by design

After the one-time model download, LokalBot works offline. Optional screenshots are sealed with AES-GCM and deleted automatically. LokalBot needs an Apple Silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later.

Get it from GitHub, and join the launch discussion on r/LocalLLaMA, especially if you have better local speech or small, fast autocomplete models to suggest.
